rewritten_text:
He wrote that he was wasting his time where he was, and that friends he had made in London were asking him to return and finish the negotiations concerning his Indian venture. He could put off leaving no longer. Since the journey to London might lead to his longer voyage even sooner than he expected, he begged me to spend as much time with him as I could. He therefore urged me to leave my lonely island and meet him in Perth, so that we could travel south together. His letter restored some of my interest in life, and I decided to leave the island in two days.

Before leaving, however, I had a task to complete that made me shudder even to consider. I had to pack my chemical instruments. This meant entering the room where I had carried out my hateful work and handling tools whose very appearance sickened me. At dawn the following morning, I gathered enough courage to unlock the laboratory door. The remains of the unfinished creature I had destroyed lay strewn across the floor, and I almost felt that I had torn apart the living flesh of a human being. I stopped to steady myself, then went inside. My hands shook as I carried the instruments out. But I realized that I must not leave the remnants of my work behind to arouse the villagers' horror and suspicion. I placed them in a basket with a large quantity of stones and set it aside, intending to throw it into the sea that same night. Meanwhile, I sat on the beach cleaning and organizing my chemical equipment.

The change in my feelings since the night of the demon's appearance could not have been more complete. Previously I had regarded my promise with bleak despair as something I was bound to fulfill, whatever the consequences. Now it seemed that a veil had been lifted from my eyes and I could see clearly for the first time. Resuming my work never entered my mind, even for an instant. His threat oppressed my thoughts, but I did not consider that I might avert it through a voluntary act of my own. I had firmly concluded that making another being like the fiend I had already created would be an act of the vilest, most appalling selfishness. I drove away every thought that might have brought me to any other conclusion.

In fact, I have left out the most important one.”

“Which is that, Harry?” the young man asked without interest.

“Oh, the natural consolation: stealing another woman's admirer after losing one's own. In fashionable society, that invariably clears a woman's reputation. But truly, Dorian, how unlike every woman we know Sibyl Vane must have been! I find something exceedingly beautiful in her death. I am pleased to inhabit a century in which such marvels occur. They persuade us that the things we all toy with—romance, passion, love—are real.”

“I treated her with terrible cruelty. You're forgetting that.”

“I fear that women value cruelty, sheer outright cruelty, above all else. Their instincts are astonishingly primitive. We have given them freedom, yet they remain slaves in search of masters. They enjoy being ruled. I'm certain you were magnificent. I've never seen you wholly and truly angry, but I can imagine how lovely you must have looked. Besides, you told me something the day before yesterday that I took then for mere fancy. Now I recognize its absolute truth; it supplies the key to the whole affair.”

“What did I say, Harry?”

“You told me that Sibyl Vane embodied every romantic heroine for you: Desdemona on one evening, Ophelia on the next; dying as Juliet, then returning to life as Imogen.”

“She won't return to life now,” the young man whispered, hiding his face in his hands.

“No, she will not live again. Her final role is finished. But regard that solitary death in the shabby dressing room simply as some strange, lurid episode from a Jacobean tragedy, a magnificent scene by Webster, Ford, or Cyril Tourneur. The girl never truly lived, and therefore never truly died. To you, at any rate, she was always a dream: a spirit passing through Shakespeare's plays and making them more beautiful by her presence, a reed that gave his music a richer, more joyous sound. The instant she encountered actual life, she spoiled it and it spoiled her, and so she vanished. Grieve over Ophelia if you wish. Scatter ashes on your head for Cordelia's strangling. Accuse Heaven because Brabantio's daughter perished. But spare your tears for Sibyl Vane. She possessed less reality than any of them.”

Silence followed. Evening deepened within the room. The shadows stole in from the garden without a sound, on silver feet, and color ebbed tiredly from the things around them.

After a while Dorian Gray raised his eyes.

Put down your weapons, fellow men, my brothers! Forgiveness, aid, and brotherly affection await your repentance. You are precious to us because you share humanity's fragile form. Every one of you will find a host and friend among these soldiers. Must man make war upon man while plague, the enemy of everyone, hangs over us already, exulting in a slaughter more savage than her own?”

Both armies hesitated. Our soldiers held their weapons tightly and regarded the enemy with stern eyes. The others still retained their arms, more through fear than any wish to fight. They glanced from one another, each longing for an example to follow, yet none would lead. Adrian sprang from his horse and went toward one of the newly slain. “He was a man,” he cried, “and now he is dead. Oh, hurry to dress the wounds of those who have fallen! Let none die. Let no more souls pass through your pitiless cuts to tell before God's throne the story of brothers murdering brothers. Bind their wounds; give them back to their friends. Banish the tiger's hearts that rage within your breasts. Cast aside these instruments of hatred and cruelty. In this respite from our destroying fate, let every man become his neighbor's brother, protector, and support. Away with those bloodied weapons! Let some of you hasten to tend these wounds.”

While speaking he knelt and lifted a man whose warm life flowed from a wound in his side. The unhappy creature gasped. Such silence had fallen over both hosts that his moaning could be plainly heard. Every heart, so recently fierce for general slaughter, now throbbed with anxious hope and fear for this one man's survival. Adrian pulled off his military scarf and wound it about the wounded man, but he was too late. The sufferer gave a long sigh; his head dropped backward, and his limbs could no longer support him. “He is dead!” Adrian said as the body slipped from his arms to the earth. He lowered his head in grief and awe. The destiny of the whole world seemed entangled in the death of that single man. The troops on either side cast down their arms. Even hardened veterans shed tears. Our men reached out their hands to their opponents, and a surge of love and profound friendship filled every breast. Unarmed, hand in hand, the two forces mingled, speaking only of ways to help each other. The enemies became one company, each side repentant: one for its earlier cruelties, the other for its recent violence. Together they followed the General's orders to march toward London.
